countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: A liquid you swallow, especially one served in a glass or a cup.
examples: Can I get you a *drink* while you wait?
They serve food and *drinks* until midnight.
No food or *drink* is allowed past this point.

gloss: A drink of any kind, especially on a menu or a label.
examples: No outside food or *beverages* are allowed in the theater.
The airline serves a complimentary *beverage* on every flight.
*Beverages* are half off before six.

gloss: A drink made by steeping or fermenting something, especially coffee or beer.
examples: She put on a fresh *brew* before the meeting.
The bar has a dozen local *brews* on the menu.
That's a strong *brew* — I'd add some milk.

gloss: Another serving of a drink poured into the same cup or glass.
examples: Would you like a *refill* on your coffee?
*Refills* are free, so help yourself.
He asked for a *refill* and went back to his book.
contrast: The stress moves: the noun is REE-fil, the verb is ree-FIL.

gloss: The feeling of needing something to drink.
examples: Nothing quenches *thirst* like cold water on a hot day.
Salty food only makes your *thirst* worse.
By the end of the hike, *thirst* was all anyone talked about.

gloss: A hot drink made by steeping dried leaves in boiling water.
examples: I drink green *tea* in the afternoon instead of coffee.
She ordered two *teas* and a scone.
The *tea* is still steeping — give it another minute.

gloss: Strong coffee made by forcing hot water through finely ground beans.
examples: He drinks a double *espresso* every morning.
That machine pulls a great *espresso*.
Two *espressos* and the check, please.
contrast: There is no x in it: espresso, never 'expresso'.

gloss: Espresso mixed with a lot of steamed milk.
examples: She stops for a *latte* on the way to work.
Can I get an oat milk *latte*, please?
Two *lattes* cost more than my lunch did.

gloss: Espresso topped with steamed and foamed milk.
examples: He ordered a *cappuccino* and sat by the window.
The *cappuccino* here comes with a little cocoa on top.
We had *cappuccinos* after dinner.
contrast: The double c sounds like ch: kap-uh-CHEE-noh.

gloss: A coffee drink flavored with chocolate.
examples: She gets a *mocha* whenever it snows.
The *mocha* was too sweet for me.
They make their *mochas* with real chocolate.
contrast: The ch is a k sound: MOH-kuh.

gloss: Coffee with the caffeine taken out.
examples: After eight I switch to *decaf*.
Is this pot regular or *decaf*?
She can't sleep unless it's *decaf*.

gloss: Black tea brewed with milk and spices.
examples: The café makes its *chai* from scratch.
I like *chai* better than plain black tea.
There's cardamom and ginger in this *chai*.

gloss: A hot drink made from chocolate powder and milk or water.
examples: The kids came in from the snow and asked for *cocoa*.
She makes *cocoa* with a pinch of salt in it.
There's a mug of *cocoa* on the counter for you.
contrast: Two syllables only, KOH-koh — the final -oa is just 'oh'.

gloss: A small paper bag of tea leaves for steeping in a cup.
examples: Leave the *tea bag* in for three minutes.
We're out of *tea bags* again.
She squeezed the *tea bag* against the spoon.

gloss: The stimulant found in coffee, tea, and many sodas.
examples: I cut out *caffeine* after lunch and started sleeping better.
There's more *caffeine* in this than in a shot of espresso.
*Caffeine* hits her hard.
contrast: Stress the second syllable, and -ei- sounds like ee: ka-FEEN.

gloss: Coffee described by how long the beans were roasted.
examples: I usually buy a medium *roast*.
They sell three *roasts*, from light to French.
This dark *roast* is way too bitter for me.

gloss: The liquid squeezed out of fruit or vegetables.
examples: He drinks orange *juice* with breakfast every day.
They sell fresh *juices* at the corner stand.
There's apple *juice* in the fridge.

gloss: A sweet fizzy soft drink.
examples: She hasn't had a *soda* in months.
We ordered a pizza and two *sodas*.
*Soda* is basically sugar and bubbles.

gloss: A fizzy soft drink, in Midwestern and Northwestern speech.
examples: Grab me a *pop* while you're up.
In Michigan they call it *pop*, not soda.
There's a cooler full of *pops* on the porch.
contrast: Regional: the Midwest says pop, the coasts say soda, and much of the South says coke.

gloss: A dark brown sweet fizzy drink.
examples: He mixes rum with *cola*.
The diner still serves *cola* in a glass bottle.
Diet *colas* all taste the same to me.

gloss: A cold nonalcoholic drink, usually sweet and fizzy.
examples: The ticket includes a hot dog and a *soft drink*.
They stopped selling *soft drinks* in the school cafeteria.
I'll just have a *soft drink*, thanks.
contrast: In everyday speech Americans say soda or pop; the British say fizzy drink.

gloss: A cold drink made from lemon juice, water, and sugar.
examples: The kids set up a *lemonade* stand on the corner.
She made a pitcher of *lemonade* for the barbecue.
Two *lemonades*, please — extra ice.
contrast: American lemonade is a still lemon drink; British lemonade is a clear fizzy soda.

gloss: Cold tea served over ice, often sweetened.
examples: She drinks unsweetened *iced tea* all summer.
Can we get two *iced teas* to go?
The *iced tea* here comes with a lemon wedge.
contrast: Written iced, not 'ice' — the -d is spelled but barely audible.

gloss: A sweet American soft drink flavored with roots and spices.
examples: *Root beer* floats were the best part of summer.
The place brews its own *root beer*.
He ordered a *root beer* and a burger.

gloss: Plain carbonated water, sometimes lightly flavored with fruit.
examples: She keeps a case of lime *seltzer* in the garage.
Can I get a *seltzer* with lime?
*Seltzer* is the only thing that got me off soda.
contrast: Americans say seltzer or sparkling water; the British say fizzy water or soda water.

gloss: A bitter fizzy mixer usually served with gin.
examples: He ordered a gin and *tonic* with extra lime.
We're out of *tonic* — use club soda.
*Tonic* has a bitterness that plain soda doesn't.

gloss: A thick cold drink of milk blended with ice cream.
examples: He got a chocolate *milkshake* with two straws.
Their *milkshakes* are so thick you need a spoon.
A burger and a *milkshake* — that's the whole menu.

gloss: A thick blended drink of fruit with ice, yogurt, or juice.
examples: She makes a *smoothie* with frozen berries every morning.
The gym sells protein *smoothies* at the counter.
This *smoothie* is more banana than anything else.

gloss: A slightly fizzy fermented tea drink.
examples: He brews his own *kombucha* in the basement.
*Kombucha* tastes like vinegar the first time you try it.
There's ginger *kombucha* on tap at the co-op.

gloss: A thick sweet liquid used to flavor drinks.
examples: Add a pump of vanilla *syrup* to the latte.
They keep a dozen flavored *syrups* behind the counter.
The drink was way too sweet — too much *syrup*.

gloss: An alcoholic drink brewed from grain and hops.
examples: He grabbed a cold *beer* out of the fridge.
We split a pitcher and a couple of *beers*.
There's *beer* in the cooler if you want one.

gloss: A beer brewed with yeast that ferments at warm temperatures.
examples: The pub has six *ales* on tap.
He prefers a brown *ale* to a lager.
This *ale* is fruitier than I expected.

gloss: A light, crisp beer fermented cold and stored before serving.
examples: A cold *lager* is perfect after mowing the lawn.
Most American *lagers* taste pretty similar to me.
She ordered a *lager* and a basket of fries.

gloss: A dark, heavy beer made with roasted malt.
examples: He nursed a *stout* by the fireplace.
The brewery is known for its chocolate *stout*.
*Stouts* are too heavy for me in the summer.

gloss: Beer served from a keg rather than from a bottle or can.
examples: They've got eight beers on *draft*.
Is the IPA on *draft* or only in bottles?
*Draft* always tastes fresher to me.
contrast: Americans spell it draft, the British draught; both sound the same.

gloss: A small metal barrel that beer is stored and served from.
examples: They tapped the *keg* around nine.
We went through three *kegs* at the party.
The *keg* is almost empty — it's mostly foam now.

gloss: A large round wooden container used to age wine or whiskey.
examples: The whiskey sat in oak *barrels* for twelve years.
They rolled the *barrel* down into the cellar.
This wine was aged in a used bourbon *barrel*.

gloss: Grain that has been sprouted and dried, used to brew beer and whiskey.
examples: You can taste the roasted *malt* in a good stout.
The brewery buys its *malt* from a farm upstate.
Single *malt* costs twice as much as a blend.

gloss: Pressed apple juice, or the alcoholic drink made from it.
examples: We bought a gallon of fresh *cider* at the orchard.
She drinks hard *cider* instead of beer.
Hot *cider* with cinnamon is a fall thing around here.
contrast: In the US, cider is unfiltered apple juice and the alcoholic kind is called hard cider; in Britain, cider is always alcoholic.

gloss: A sparkling white wine, usually served at celebrations.
examples: They opened a bottle of *champagne* at midnight.
There's *champagne* chilling in the ice bucket.
We toasted the couple with *champagne*.
contrast: The ch is sh and the stress falls on the second syllable: sham-PAYN.

gloss: A strong fortified wine from southern Spain.
examples: Her grandmother kept a bottle of *sherry* in the cabinet.
The recipe calls for a splash of dry *sherry*.
They served *sherry* before dinner.

gloss: A fortified wine flavored with herbs, used mostly in cocktails.
examples: A martini is mostly gin with a little *vermouth*.
Keep the *vermouth* in the fridge once it's open.
He poured out the *vermouth* and swirled the glass.
contrast: Stress the second syllable: vur-MOOTH.

gloss: A field where grapes are grown for wine.
examples: They bought a small *vineyard* in Sonoma.
The *vineyards* turn gold in October.
He walked us through the *vineyard* before the tasting.
contrast: Short first syllable, VIN-yurd, even though it's spelled with vine.

gloss: A place where wine is made and often sold.
examples: We toured three *wineries* in one afternoon.
The *winery* opens for tastings at eleven.
She works at a small family *winery*.

gloss: The year in which a wine's grapes were harvested.
examples: Nineteen eighty-two was a famous *vintage*.
He can name the *vintage* just by tasting it.
Older *vintages* cost a fortune.

gloss: An underground room where wine is stored.
examples: The restaurant keeps two thousand bottles in its *cellar*.
He went down to the *cellar* for another bottle.
Their wine *cellar* stays cool all summer.
contrast: Sounds exactly like seller.

gloss: The substance in beer, wine, and liquor that makes people drunk.
examples: He gave up *alcohol* in January.
There's no *alcohol* at the reception.
The label says fourteen percent *alcohol*.

ru: крепкий алкоголь (водка, виски и т. п.)
gloss: Strong distilled alcohol such as vodka, whiskey, or rum.
examples: The store sells beer and wine but no *liquor*.
He keeps the *liquor* on the top shelf.
They ran out of *liquor* before midnight.
contrast: Spelled -quor but pronounced LIK-ur; don't confuse it with liqueur (lih-KUR), which is sweet.

gloss: A sweet, strongly flavored alcoholic drink usually sipped after a meal.
examples: She poured a coffee *liqueur* over the ice cream.
The shelf was full of fruit *liqueurs*.
This *liqueur* is far too sweet to drink straight.
contrast: A near-twin of liquor on paper only: liqueur is lih-KUR and sweet, liquor is LIK-ur and strong.

gloss: Alcoholic drink, in casual speech.
examples: Somebody needs to bring the *booze*.
There was plenty of food but not much *booze*.
He swore off *booze* for a year.

gloss: A strong drink distilled from grain and aged in wooden barrels.
examples: He takes his *whiskey* neat.
The bar carries forty different *whiskeys*.
A little *whiskey* in the coffee wouldn't hurt.
contrast: American and Irish makers spell it whiskey; Scottish and Canadian makers spell it whisky.

gloss: An American whiskey made mostly from corn.
examples: He poured two fingers of *bourbon*.
Most *bourbon* comes out of Kentucky.
They aged the *bourbon* for eight years.
contrast: Say BUR-bun, not 'bor-BON'.

gloss: A clear, nearly tasteless spirit distilled from grain or potatoes.
examples: She keeps the *vodka* in the freezer.
*Vodka* and soda is her usual drink.
They had us taste four different *vodkas*.

gloss: A clear spirit flavored with juniper berries.
examples: He ordered a *gin* and tonic.
*Gin* tastes like a pine tree to me.
The bar makes its own *gin* in the back.
contrast: The g is soft — jin, not a hard g.

gloss: A spirit distilled from sugarcane or molasses.
examples: He mixed dark *rum* with pineapple juice.
There's *rum* in the cake, so watch out.
The shop stocks aged *rums* from all over the Caribbean.

gloss: A Mexican spirit distilled from the agave plant.
examples: One more *tequila* and I'm going home.
Good *tequila* is meant to be sipped, not shot.
They lined up four *tequilas* on the bar.
contrast: The qu is just a k sound: tuh-KEE-luh.

gloss: A strong drink distilled from wine or fruit.
examples: He warmed his hands around a glass of *brandy*.
She added a spoonful of *brandy* to the sauce.
The shop stocks several French *brandies*.

gloss: A fine brandy from a region of western France.
examples: They finished the meal with *cognac*.
He keeps an expensive *cognac* for guests.
That *cognac* was older than I am.
contrast: The gn sounds like ny: KOHN-yak.

gloss: A Japanese alcoholic drink brewed from rice.
examples: They served the *sake* warm in tiny cups.
*Sake* goes well with sushi.
He ordered a bottle of cold *sake*.
contrast: Two syllables, SAH-kee — not like the sake in 'for heaven's sake'.

gloss: Strong homemade liquor produced illegally.
examples: His grandfather made *moonshine* in the woods.
That *moonshine* could strip paint.
They hid the *moonshine* under the floorboards.

gloss: A factory where spirits such as whiskey are made.
examples: We toured a *distillery* outside Louisville.
The *distillery* hands out samples at the end.
Several small *distilleries* have opened downtown.

gloss: A place where beer is made.
examples: There's a new *brewery* on Third Street.
The *brewery* serves food until ten.
Local *breweries* have taken over the neighborhood.

gloss: A mixed drink of liquor with juice, soda, or other flavors.
examples: She ordered a *cocktail* with grapefruit and gin.
*Cocktails* are half price until seven.
He makes a mean *cocktail*.

gloss: A cocktail of gin or vodka with a little vermouth.
examples: He likes his *martini* with three olives.
Two *martinis* and I'm done for the night.
The *martini* came out in a chilled glass.

gloss: A tequila cocktail made with lime and served with salt on the rim.
examples: They ordered a pitcher of *margaritas*.
Her *margarita* came with salt around the rim.
Frozen *margaritas* give me a headache.

gloss: A Cuban cocktail of rum, lime, sugar, and mint.
examples: He muddled mint for the *mojitos*.
A cold *mojito* on the porch is summer to me.
Their *mojito* is more soda than rum.
contrast: The Spanish j sounds like h: moh-HEE-toh.

gloss: A Spanish drink of red wine mixed with fruit and juice.
examples: She made a pitcher of *sangria* for the party.
The *sangria* had orange slices floating in it.
We split a pitcher of white *sangria*.

gloss: A sweet drink of juice mixed in a large bowl, sometimes with alcohol.
examples: Somebody spiked the *punch*.
There's *punch* and cookies in the back.
She ladled *punch* into paper cups.

gloss: A thick holiday drink of milk, eggs, sugar, and often rum.
examples: He drinks *eggnog* straight from the carton in December.
The *eggnog* had a little too much rum in it.
Stores start stocking *eggnog* right after Thanksgiving.

gloss: A drink taken just before going to bed.
examples: They had a *nightcap* by the fire.
Come up for a *nightcap*.
One *nightcap* turned into three.

ru: безалкогольный компонент коктейля (сок, тоник и т. п.)
gloss: A nonalcoholic drink added to liquor in a cocktail.
examples: We have the vodka but no *mixers*.
Cranberry juice is the only *mixer* in the house.
Pick up some *mixers* on your way over.

gloss: A mild drink swallowed right after a shot of liquor.
examples: He took the shot and grabbed a beer as a *chaser*.
Can I get a water *chaser* with that?
*Chasers* make the whiskey go down easier.

gloss: A sweet fizzy soft drink flavored with ginger.
examples: Flight attendants pour a lot of *ginger ale*.
She drinks *ginger ale* when her stomach is upset.
Two *ginger ales* and a coffee, please.

gloss: A small piece of fruit or herb added to a drink for looks and flavor.
examples: The *garnish* was a twist of orange peel.
He lined up the *garnishes* before the dinner rush.
Skip the *garnish* — I just want the drink.

gloss: A metal container for mixing a cocktail with ice.
examples: He rattled the *shaker* for a good ten seconds.
The bar had two *shakers* going at once.
Pour it straight out of the *shaker* through a strainer.

gloss: A large cup with a handle, used for hot drinks.
examples: He drinks out of the same chipped *mug* every morning.
The cupboard is full of *mugs* from other cities.
She warmed her hands on the *mug*.

gloss: A glass with a stem, made for drinking wine.
examples: She rinsed the *wineglasses* by hand.
He knocked over a *wineglass* reaching for the bread.
The *wineglass* was filled a little too full.

gloss: A straight-sided drinking glass with no stem or handle.
examples: He poured the whiskey into a heavy *tumbler*.
We drink water out of old jars and *tumblers*.
The *tumbler* left a ring on the table.

gloss: A very small glass holding a single measure of liquor.
examples: He collects *shot glasses* from every state he visits.
Fill the *shot glass* to the line.
She measured the syrup with a *shot glass*.

gloss: A large container with a handle and a spout for pouring drinks.
examples: They brought out a *pitcher* of iced tea.
We ordered a *pitcher* for the table.
There are two *pitchers* of water on the counter.
contrast: Americans say pitcher where the British say jug.

gloss: A big container with a narrow mouth and a handle.
examples: He carried a *jug* of water out to the field.
We bought a *jug* of cider at the farm.
Empty *jugs* were stacked by the door.

gloss: An open glass container for serving wine or water at the table.
examples: They left a *carafe* of water on the table.
We ordered a half *carafe* of the house red.
The *carafe* was already empty.

gloss: A flat pocket bottle for carrying liquor.
examples: He had a *flask* in his coat pocket.
She filled the *flask* before the game.
Someone passed a *flask* around at halftime.
contrast: American English uses the vowel of cat; British English uses the long ah of father.

gloss: A pot with a spout and a lid for brewing and pouring tea.
examples: She warmed the *teapot* before adding the leaves.
The *teapot* has a chip on the spout.
He set two *teapots* on the tray.

gloss: A covered pot used to boil water.
examples: Put the *kettle* on, would you?
The *kettle* started whistling.
We keep an electric *kettle* next to the sink.

gloss: The small plate a cup sits on.
examples: He set the cup back down on the *saucer*.
The *saucers* don't match the cups.
Coffee had spilled into the *saucer*.

gloss: A machine that brews coffee automatically.
examples: The *coffeemaker* starts at six every morning.
Our *coffeemaker* finally died last week.
Hotel rooms all have those tiny *coffeemakers*.

gloss: An electric machine that mixes drinks and crushes ice.
examples: She threw everything into the *blender*.
The *blender* woke up the whole house.
You need a strong *blender* for frozen drinks.

gloss: An insulated box for keeping drinks cold.
examples: The beer's in the *cooler* on the porch.
We packed two *coolers* for the drive.
Somebody left the *cooler* open all night.

gloss: A thin tube for drinking from a glass or cup.
examples: Can I get a *straw* with that?
The café switched to paper *straws*.
He was chewing on his *straw* the whole time.

gloss: A small mat that a glass sits on to protect the table.
examples: Use a *coaster*, please.
The bar's *coasters* have the logo printed on them.
She slid a *coaster* under his glass.

gloss: A cover that fits on top of a cup or container.
examples: The *lid* wasn't on tight and it spilled.
He snapped a *lid* onto the to-go cup.
The *lids* are over by the milk and sugar.

gloss: The stopper in the neck of a wine bottle.
examples: The *cork* broke off in the bottle.
He smelled the *cork* out of habit.
She saves the *corks* in a big jar.

gloss: A tool for pulling corks out of bottles.
examples: Does anybody have a *corkscrew*?
The *corkscrew* is in the drawer by the stove.
He got the wine open without a *corkscrew*.

gloss: The valve that beer is poured from at a bar.
examples: They have twenty beers on *tap*.
The bartender cleaned the *taps* before opening.
This one's fresh off the *tap*.

gloss: The fixture that water comes out of at a sink.
examples: He filled the glass straight from the *faucet*.
The kitchen *faucet* is dripping again.
Both *faucets* need new washers.
contrast: Americans say faucet; the British say tap.

gloss: The thick fatty part of milk, often added to coffee.
examples: I take my coffee with *cream* and no sugar.
There's *cream* in the door of the fridge.
He poured a little *cream* into the mug.

gloss: Frozen water, added to drinks to make them cold.
examples: Can I get that with no *ice*?
There's *ice* in the freezer.
The *ice* melted and watered down my drink.

gloss: The layer of tiny bubbles on top of a drink.
examples: That beer was mostly *foam*.
She likes extra *foam* on her cappuccino.
*Foam* spilled over the rim of the glass.

gloss: The bubbles and hiss of a carbonated drink.
examples: The soda lost its *fizz* overnight.
There's still a little *fizz* left in it.
I like the *fizz* more than the flavor.

gloss: A small ball of gas rising through a liquid.
examples: *Bubbles* rose to the top of the glass.
Champagne has finer *bubbles* than soda.
He watched a single *bubble* drift up the side.

gloss: A small amount of drink taken into the mouth at once.
examples: She took a *sip* and made a face.
He finished the whole cup in tiny *sips*.
One *sip* was enough to tell it had gone bad.

gloss: A large swallow of a drink.
examples: He drank the water in three *gulps*.
She took a *gulp* of coffee and ran for the door.
One long *gulp* and the glass was empty.

gloss: A big mouthful drunk straight from a bottle.
examples: He took a *swig* from the bottle and passed it on.
She had a quick *swig* of water between songs.
A couple of *swigs* later, the flask was empty.

gloss: A small serving of strong liquor or espresso drunk at once.
examples: They each did a *shot* of tequila.
Two *shots* of espresso, please.
He ordered a beer and a *shot*.

gloss: A measure of about half a liter, the usual glass of beer.
examples: He ordered a *pint* of the local IPA.
Two *pints* and we called it a night.
A *pint* of milk costs next to nothing here.
contrast: Say PYNT, with the vowel of pie — not like mint or hint.

gloss: An American measure of liquid equal to two pints.
examples: Pick up a *quart* of milk on your way home.
The recipe calls for two *quarts* of cider.
They only had the small *quart* size left.

gloss: An American measure of liquid equal to four quarts.
examples: We go through a *gallon* of juice a week.
He bought two *gallons* of water for the trip.
A *gallon* of milk is heavier than it looks.

gloss: A metric measure of liquid, a little more than a quart.
examples: The bottle holds two *liters*.
Doctors tell you to drink about two *liters* of water a day.
A *liter* is a little more than a quart.
contrast: American spelling liter; British spelling litre.

gloss: A drink bought for everyone in the group at the same time.
examples: This *round* is on me.
They bought three *rounds* before dinner even arrived.
It's your turn to get the next *round*.

gloss: Six cans or bottles of a drink sold together.
examples: Grab a *six-pack* on your way over.
He brought two *six-packs* to the cookout.
A *six-pack* of that costs twelve bucks now.

gloss: Someone who mixes and serves drinks at a bar.
examples: The *bartender* remembered my order.
She worked as a *bartender* all through college.
Two *bartenders* were handling the whole room.

gloss: Someone who makes coffee drinks in a café.
examples: The *barista* spelled my name wrong again.
He trained as a *barista* in Seattle.
Two *baristas* were working the morning rush.

gloss: A small place that serves coffee and light food.
examples: There's a *café* on the corner with good pastries.
She writes at the same *café* every afternoon.
The *cafés* downtown all close by six.
contrast: Americans stress the second syllable, ka-FAY; the British often say CAF-ay.

gloss: A place that serves beer and simple food.
examples: We met at a *pub* near the station.
The *pub* has trivia night on Wednesdays.
There are three *pubs* on this block alone.

gloss: The early-evening stretch when a bar sells drinks cheap.
examples: *Happy hour* runs from four to six.
We got there just in time for *happy hour*.
Their *happy hour* prices are the best downtown.

gloss: A running bill for drinks that you settle when you leave.
examples: Can I start a *tab*?
He closed out his *tab* and left.
Put it on my *tab*.

gloss: A short speech made before everyone drinks together.
examples: Her brother gave the *toast* at the wedding.
Let's raise a glass and make a *toast*.
There were three *toasts* before the food came out.

gloss: The headache and sickness that follow drinking too much.
examples: He woke up with a terrible *hangover*.
Water before bed helps with the *hangover*.
*Hangovers* get worse as you get older.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The particular taste of a food or drink.
examples: This soda comes in six *flavors*.
The tea lost its *flavor* after sitting out all night.
Cherry is my favorite *flavor*.
contrast: American spelling flavor; British spelling flavour.

gloss: A strong pleasant smell, especially of food or drink.
examples: The *aroma* of fresh coffee filled the kitchen.
This wine has an *aroma* of cherry and smoke.
Different *aromas* come out as it warms up.
